common_name: German Extra Hardy Garlic (Robust Cold-Climate Porcelain Hardneck)
scientific_name: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'German Extra Hardy'

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so roots establish before dormancy; German Extra Hardy is a porcelain hardneck bred for exceptional winter survival and needs a real cold period to form well-divided bulbs, making it best suited to zone 3-7.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. German Extra Hardy is one of the most popular and reliable porcelain hardneck garlics for cold-climate gardeners, prized for its outstanding winter hardiness and consistent production of large bulbs with 4-5 big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, sometimes with faint purple streaking. Flavor is strong and full-bodied raw, mellowing to a rich, savory sweetness when roasted. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location, then trim and store; German Extra Hardy has only moderate storage life, typically 4-6 months, so use it earlier in the year relative to longer-storing softneck types.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Garlic

common_name: Spanish Roja Garlic (Classic Rocambole with Superior Flavor)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Spanish Roja is a rocambole-type hardneck with a strong cold requirement for good bulb formation, best suited to zone 3-7 with a real winter chill.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Spanish Roja is a classic rocambole-type hardneck garlic, brought to the Pacific Northwest by Spanish settlers generations ago, and widely considered by garlic growers and chefs to have some of the finest, most complex flavor of any garlic variety — rich, hot, and full without being harsh. Bulbs have a distinctive rich reddish-brown skin over 8-12 large, very easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it produces a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. The main tradeoff for its superior flavor is shorter storage life than porcelain or softneck types, typically only 4-5 months, so plan to use Spanish Roja earlier in the storage season. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

common_name: Korean Red Garlic (Vigorous Cold-Hardy Asiatic Hardneck)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Korean Red is an Asiatic-type hardneck that needs a real winter chill to form well-divided bulbs and performs best in zone 3-7.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Korean Red is a vigorous Asiatic-type hardneck garlic prized for its early maturity, reliable productivity, and strong, spicy-hot flavor with a pleasant lingering sweetness once cooked. Bulbs are medium-sized with glossy, deep reddish-purple-streaked skin and 6-10 cloves, and the plants tend to size up and mature earlier in the season than many other hardneck types, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early garlic harvest. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect energy into the bulb; the scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Harvest bulbs once the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming and storing; like most hardnecks, storage life is moderate, around 4-6 months.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997
